definition: Expedient means convenient and advantageous for oneself, putting practicality ahead of principle.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word expedient. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know expedient should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Trading the star pitcher felt expedient at the deadline — the payroll shrank, the owners cheered, and the fans paid for it all September.
Sensible stays milder than expedient — the sensible choice simply works, with nothing traded away to get it; expedient buys the win by bending a principle.
Ruthless goes further than expedient — the expedient choice bends a principle for advantage; the ruthless one tramples people and never looks down.

Convenient means easy and suitable — the option that saves time and trouble — and it carries no shadow at all. Expedient is convenience with a bill attached: the choice serves the chooser's advantage while a principle or someone else quietly pays. When nobody is shortchanged, convenient is the honest word.

Self-serving names the motive outright — the choice benefits the chooser, full stop — and drops any claim of practicality. Expedient keeps both halves: the move genuinely works right now, and it works chiefly for whoever chose it. A self-serving decision may not even solve the problem it answers.

Offered a way out of a scheduling crunch, the network made the expedient call: it aired the finale unfinished, visual effects and all, to beat a rival's premiere.
Ratings won the night; the apology, the patched rerun, and the animators' resignations filled the month that followed.

Expedient is the exact word because it means convenient and advantageous, especially when serving one's own interest — the choice that works right now, with the cost quietly shipped to later or to someone else.
Practical solves the problem; expedient serves the chooser, and the word usually arrives with an eyebrow raised.
Expedient grades a choice by convenience rather than principle, so it carries a raised eyebrow — editorials love it.
Beside its unit-mates: prudence weighs long-term consequences, where expedient dodges them; facile is the lazy argument, expedient the lazy ethics.
When no self-interest shades the choice, plain convenient is the honest label.

Facing a printing deadline and a half-empty front page, the editor of the Millbrook Gazette made an expedient call: she ran the mayor's press release word for word.
It worked, in every short-term way a decision can work.
The page was full by nine, the printer was paid on time, and the mayor's office was delighted.
The release skipped the budget shortfall entirely, and the Gazette's readers never learned of it.
A rival weekly ran the shortfall story two days later and picked up four hundred of her subscribers.
Years afterward she used the episode to teach interns the difference between a fix that is easy and a fix that is honest.
